title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning, and happy Thanksgiving! Today's digest leans on 2026 systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and RCTs across your tracked topics — anti-aging supplements, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. The recurring theme this cycle: reputable sources are tempering the hype, favoring interventions with human RCTs and honest effect sizes. Citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This cycle's message from the research community: **no supplement has human proof of extending lifespan**, and the gap between lab hype and clinical data is still wide.

- **Head-to-head on the big three.** A 2026 comparative review (*J. of Biosciences and Medicines*) lined up **urolithin A**, **spermidine**, and **NAD+ precursors (NR/NMN)**. Verdict: **urolithin A** has the most coherent translational profile — aligned mechanism, biomarker, and early functional data for mitochondrial health, muscle endurance, and immune aging (≈10 human randomized studies, ~492 participants). **NR/NMN** reliably *raise NAD+ biomarkers* but show inconsistent anti-aging outcomes; **spermidine** remains biologically plausible but clinically unvalidated.
- **How much evidence, really?** An October 2026 audit of **19 popular longevity supplements** found **none** is FDA-approved or guideline-recommended for aging. Only **berberine, omega-3s, and vitamin D** reach "large human studies"; the other 16 rest on small trials. For 18 of 19, animal/lab studies vastly outnumber human RCTs (e.g., **taurine**: ~323 lab studies vs. 4 RCTs).
- **Taurine deflated.** An NIH/NIA analysis found **huge variation** in blood taurine between adults and **no clear link** between taurine levels and health status — undercutting the "taurine deficiency drives aging" story.
- **One to watch.** The NIH/NIA **urolithin A × glucose-metabolism RCT (NCT06274749, 180 adults 55+)** is set to begin recruiting **November 30, 2026**, testing whether UA improves beta-cell insulin response.

Practical framing: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "longevity" claims as marketing until proven otherwise.

sections.body:
Fresh 2026 meta-analyses keep HIIT as a **time-efficient cardio and fat-loss tool** for women — with a consistent caveat to **add resistance training** for strength and function.

- **Middle-aged & older women.** A 2026 systematic review & meta-analysis in *Frontiers in Physiology* (**19 RCTs**) found HIIT significantly improves **VO₂max (SMD = 1.20, high certainty)**, but had **limited effect on muscle strength**, flexibility, or sit-to-stand. Walking ability improved only borderline. Bottom line: *HIIT alone is insufficient to comprehensively improve functional fitness.*
- **Overweight/obese women.** Another 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* meta-analysis (**15 RCTs**) found HIIT significantly reduced **body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass**, and strongly improved **VO₂max (g = 1.09)**. Effects on cholesterol/triglycerides were **uncertain** (low certainty) — expect recomposition more than dramatic lipid shifts.
- **PCOS.** A network meta-analysis (**23 RCTs, ~1,192 women**) ranked **HIIT best** for raising VO₂max and lowering **fasting insulin** and **LDL**, while **moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)** ranked best for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). A blended week may cover both.
- **Postmenopausal lipids.** A dose-response network meta-analysis (**51 RCTs**) ranked HIIT highest for **triglyceride reduction** — but the HIIT estimate rested on only **3 studies**, so treat it as suggestive, not settled.

Bottom line: intensity drives cardio and metabolic wins; **pair HIIT with strength work**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). New 2026 trials sharpen two points: **supervision matters**, and **targeted add-ons help the hardest cases**.

- **Supervised beats home-alone.** A 2026 RCT (60 women with confirmed SUI) found **supervised PFMT** cut pad-test leakage from **22.9 g → 3.2 g** (p < 0.001) vs. a non-significant **25.7 g → 17.8 g** for unsupervised home training. Supervised patients also hit Oxford grade 4–5 strength far more often (**66.7% vs. 13.3%**). Unsupervised PFMT still helps *if* adherence is high — but guided programs win.
- **PFMT > Pilates.** A three-arm RCT (105 women) in the *International Urogynecology Journal* found **PFMT superior to Pilates** (± voluntary pelvic-floor contraction) across the board: incontinence-impact score dropped **−4.4 (PFMT) vs. −0.7 (Pilates)**, with much larger gains in strength and vaginal squeeze pressure. Pilates is a nice adjunct, not a substitute.
- **Very weak pelvic floor? Add stimulation.** A multicentre, double-blind RCT (*EJOG*) added **sEMG-triggered intravaginal electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT in women with SUI and very weak muscles. The stimulation group had **earlier, greater, and longer-lasting** gains — at 12 months: **−1.5 leaks/week, −2.6 pads/day, −5.2 ICIQ-SF points**, with 65% reporting meaningful improvement vs. 18% of controls.

Key point: **correct technique, supervision, and consistency** beat sheer reps. Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" as evidence-based integrative care that runs **alongside** standard HER2-targeted therapy — **not** a replacement. The honest 2026 picture: promising mechanisms, thin clinical proof, and real interaction risks.

- **Correct vitamin D deficiency — plausibly helpful.** A 2026 retrospective interventional study (*Nutrients*, 196 curative-intent HER2+ patients) found those who **repleted** vitamin D had **numerically better 3-year disease-free survival (90% vs. 85%)**, and failing to correct deficiency carried a **1.7× higher recurrence hazard** (not statistically significant here, but matching a significant prior cohort; two 2025 RCTs reported a **doubling of pathologic complete response** with repletion, strongest in HER2+/triple-negative). Genetics context: **TP53 mutations occur in 55–75% of HER2+ tumors**, and **germline TP53 (Li-Fraumeni) carriers develop HER2+ disease ~67%** of the time — so p53 status is central to this group.
- **Omega-3 / DHA — unproven so far.** The phase-II double-blind **DHA-WIN** RCT (DHA 4.4 g/day during neoadjuvant chemo) found **no added Ki-67 benefit** overall (only a non-significant HER2+ trend) and no survival signal. A July 2026 systematic review of omega-3 during chemo rated efficacy evidence **"very low certainty"** and independent benefit **unproven** — though generally well tolerated.
- **Curcumin & polyphenols — mechanism, not proof.** A 2026 critical review found curcumin has **testable signals but no replicated recurrence/survival benefit**; one promising 2025 trial used a **piperine bioenhancer with known drug-interaction potential**. Green-tea catechins modulate **p53 signaling** in the lab, but effects **depend on wild-type vs. mutant p53** and remain preclinical.

Important framing: much of this is **early or observational**. Fixing a documented vitamin D deficiency is reasonable; otherwise, **coordinate every supplement with your oncology team** — interactions with targeted therapy are a genuine concern.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance is unchanged and firm: **behavioral therapy first, pills second, supplements rarely.**

- **CBT-I is first-line — full stop.** The 2026 *Nature Reviews Disease Primers* on insomnia and the current **VA/DoD guideline** both put **cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)** ahead of medication, with **digital CBT-I** offering a scalable option. Core components for *fragmented* sleep: **sleep restriction** (match time-in-bed to actual sleep to build sleep drive), **stimulus control** (bed = sleep only), and **arousal reduction** (wind-down, relaxation).
- **If you need a drug, newer class is better-tolerated.** Guidelines suggest **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** — daridorexant, lemborexant, suvorexant — among first-choice agents; AASM specifically suggests **suvorexant for sleep-maintenance insomnia**. A 2026 phase-II PSG analysis showed **daridorexant dose-dependently reduced awakenings (NAW) and wake-after-sleep-onset**, cutting fragmentation and restoring deeper **N3 and REM** sleep — directly relevant to disjointed sleep. Older **Z-drugs/benzodiazepines** stay short-term only.
- **Supplements, honestly.** The VA/DoD guideline **suggests against** routine **melatonin** (and valerian, chamomile, etc.) for chronic insomnia. For **magnesium**, a brand-new 2026 systematic review (**12 RCTs**, *J. Dietary Supplements*) concluded current evidence **does not support routine use** — only modest, inconsistent subjective benefit in some adults (low certainty).

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and start **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
